content.text: Swift doesn’t like errors to happen when your program runs, which means it won’t let you run an error-throwing function by accident.

Instead, you need to call these functions using three new keywords: `do` starts a section of code that might cause problems, `try` is used before every function that might throw an error, and `catch` lets you handle errors gracefully.
If any errors are thrown inside the `do` block, execution immediately jumps to the `catch` block. Let’s try calling `checkPassword()` with a parameter that throws an error:
When that code runs, “You can’t use that password” is printed, but “That password is good” won’t be – that code will never be reached, because the error is thrown.

title: Running throwing functions
postscript: You can have multiple catch blocks to handle individual errors if you want, but you do need to catch all possible errors at some point otherwise your code won't build.
question: Which of the following are true?
hint: Start a throwing block using `do`, mark each throwing line with `try` and catch errors using `catch`.

correct.answer: Throwing functions must be called using `try`
Throwing functions must be marked with `throws`
Swift won't let you run an error-throwing function by accident.
Use `do` to start a section of code that calls throwing functions.
If any errors are thrown, execution immediately jumps to the `catch` block.
You can mark any function as throwing.

wrong.reason: They can return values just like regular functions.

wrong.answer: You can call only one throwing function inside a `do` block.
wrong.reason: You can call as many as you want.

wrong.answer: Swift lets you skip adding a `catch` block when it's safe.
wrong.reason: If functions throw errors, you must catch those errors.

wrong.answer: You don't need to catch all errors.
wrong.reason: If functions throw errors, you must catch those errors.

wrong.answer: You should mark all functions as throwing.
wrong.reason: There's no need for this – only mark functions as throwing if they throw errors.

wrong.answer: You can define only one error enum in your apps.
wrong.reason: You can define as many as you need.
